name: Gareth Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This interview is confidential. What does an ordinary day at the contact centre look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, have a two-year college diploma, and lead the account-access calls when a customer cannot get into an order. I am good at spotting which failed login is a typo and which needs a careful check. I use AI every day to sort long chat histories, but I make the decision from the account record. The pay is low for a lead desk.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What comes home with you after a shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Tessa and I have two children in school and a mortgage. She works at a small repair shop; between us we have about three weeks of expenses saved. There are few other centres near us. I like showing a new agent how to ask one useful question instead of reading a script twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau sounds like the sorter we already use, handy but no miracle. I would keep making the last account check myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead calls stay useful here. The three-week reserve is the problem, because one car repair could swallow it and Tessa needs that car for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading access calls and checking AI summaries against the login record. In the first year of small change, I’d put the cost of our Sunday shop snack into savings each week instead of buying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the car and the mortgage, steady about the work. An AI message sorter cannot tell a frightened customer why their own account locked them out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a trainee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would point the new agent to the failed-login times. A summary can say 'customer upset' without showing the fifth failed attempt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes on Sunday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children our Sunday walk is still on, just without the snack counter. That keeps the habit and saves a little money.

say: I’d call the **AI sorter** useful only beside the account record.
I’d tell agents to keep the **last account check** with a person.
think: I think my **lead calls** remain useful in this mild world.
I worry a **car repair** could empty our three-week reserve.
do: Keep **leading access calls** and checking AI summaries against login records.
Skip the **Sunday snack** and transfer its cost to savings weekly while keeping the family walk.
feel: **Uneasy** about household bills, steady about work.
S0.quote: An AI message sorter cannot tell a frightened customer why their own account locked them out.
fieldNote: He trusts **account evidence** more than a tidy summary.
The **car** supports Tessa’s work and threatens their thin reserve.
He keeps the **family walk** while cutting its small extra cost.

steps.text: Keep leading access calls and check AI summaries against login records
Save the cost of the Sunday snack each week for mortgage bills
Skip the Sunday snack counter while keeping the family walk

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will swallow password questions before it touches the tricky account locks. I would ask for the new rota and actual error count before I call the change a win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can handle exceptions, but a smaller queue could still mean fewer paid lead hours. I cannot count on a nearby centre hiring me when so few are close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new access-check AI on a paid shift by running fifteen old lock cases through it and comparing the proposed unlock with the account log. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid account-security role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover our mortgage, keeping my current desk until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I want to see the cases myself. If the access-check AI misses one stolen account, a fast average is no comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which old case matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would include the case where the delivery address changed five minutes before the login failed. That detail is easy to lose in a short summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your wife check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Tessa (my wife) the hours column beside the rate. A title with fewer shifts cannot carry the house.

say: I’d say **password chats** may move before complex account locks.
I’d ask for **error counts** and paid hours before praising the new system.
think: I think my **exception skill** remains valuable for a while.
I fear **lead hours** could shrink with the queue.
do: Learn the **access-check AI** through fifteen old cases on paid time in 2026.
Apply for **posted security work** only with written mortgage-covering weekly wage and hours; stay until signed offer.
feel: **Anxious**, but ready to test actual cases.
S1.quote: If the access-check AI misses one stolen account, a fast average is no comfort.
fieldNote: He learns through **old account locks**, not a sales demonstration.
The **few local centres** limit an easy switch.
He needs **whole-week pay**, not just a stronger title.

steps.text: Learn access-check AI by testing fifteen old lock cases against logs on paid shift
Apply for posted account-security work with written mortgage-covering pay/hours; stay until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could run even the hard access calls. I would ask management for written dates and posted paid jobs rather than a speech about resilience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the headset may stop paying before I find another lead desk. Robots around 2031 are later and irrelevant to a login call; our three-week cushion is too short for a slow vacancy process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d cancel the planned new television and bank that money. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid account-security job only if written wage and hours cover our mortgage; I’d keep the current job until a signed offer and take its required course only if funded on paid time. If a first wage is delayed despite the offer, I’d ask my brother for at most one mortgage payment and agree on a repayment date before taking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and doing the arithmetic before panic takes over. A three-week reserve cannot bridge a three-month hiring process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why delay the television?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Tessa (my wife) our old television still works. If it fails, we can decide then; I will not spend the replacement money now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How certain is your brother’s help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother Leon has helped our parents with a bill before, but I cannot assume he has spare cash. I would ask only after a signed job offer and only for one mortgage payment, with a date to repay.

say: I’d say **2028 AGI** may take hard access calls too.
I’d ask for **written dates** and posted paid jobs before cuts.
think: I think my **headset wage** could go before another lead vacancy appears.
I know **three weeks saved** cannot cover a slow search.
do: Cancel the **television purchase** and bank its price in 2026.
Seek **posted security work** after 2028 with written mortgage-covering pay/hours; take required funded course on paid time; stay until signed offer.
Ask **brother Leon** for one mortgage payment only after signed offer if pay lags, with a repayment date.
S2.quote: A three-week reserve cannot bridge a three-month hiring process.
fieldNote: He sees **2028 thinking AI** as the headset deadline.
His **brother’s help** is uncertain, capped and tied to a signed offer.
The course needs **funded paid time** for a posted vacancy.

steps.text: Cancel planned television purchase and bank its price while current set works
Apply for posted security work after 2028 with written mortgage-covering pay/hours; stay until signed offer
Take required funded security course on paid time only for posted paid job
Ask brother Leon for one mortgage payment after signed offer if pay lags; agree repayment date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives enough time to test whether the security desk is real paid work. I would tell newer agents not to buy a course from a promise on a noticeboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could qualify for a security role before 2031 if it exists, although full AGI may do much of its checking too. Tessa and I need a bigger reserve before any change of hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d take an employer-funded account-security course on paid time only if a posted paid vacancy requires it. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for that posted role only with written weekly wage and hours that cover our mortgage, keeping my access desk until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but five years gives me time to refuse a bad offer. I cannot pay a mortgage with a security-course badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to practise tracing an address change through a real training account. Reading slides about fraud would not prove I can stop the wrong unlock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you build a reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set aside a fixed amount after each pay, even if it starts small. We can review it with the mortgage book once a month.

say: I’d ask for **real paid security vacancies** before training.
I’d warn new agents against **course promises** without a job.
think: I think I could qualify for **security work** before 2031.
I know **full AGI** could threaten security checks as well.
do: Take **funded security training** on paid time only if required for a posted paid vacancy.
Save a **fixed amount** from each wage starting in 2026.
Apply for **posted security work** after 2031 with written mortgage-covering weekly wage and hours; stay until signed offer.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to reject weak offers.
S3.quote: I cannot pay a mortgage with a security-course badge.
fieldNote: He wants **address-change practice** in the course.
He ties **training** to paid time and a posted role.
A **fixed saving** can start small while work continues.

steps.text: Take employer-funded security course on paid time only if a posted paid vacancy requires it
Save a fixed amount from each pay for the mortgage reserve
Apply for posted security role after 2031 with written mortgage-covering pay/hours; stay until signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us years to teach trainees how to verify a locked account, not just click an answer. I would keep a paid shadow shift for each new agent if the centre lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can keep earning and save a decent reserve before 2036, though cheap thinking AI could still take the whole access desk. Robots around 2039 are no shield for my screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep leading access calls and transfer a fixed amount from each pay into savings. In the first year after 2036, I’d seek posted paid security work only if my hours fall and the written weekly wage and hours cover our mortgage, keeping my desk until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long end, worried enough about this month’s bills to stay disciplined. A decade before AGI helps only if I still bring a wage home each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a trainee do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let a trainee listen to one hard call on a paid shift, then ask what in the account record changed their mind. That is how I learned from my first lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children in their school. We would only consider a move if Tessa (my wife) and I had a signed offer with mortgage-covering pay after travel and housing costs.

say: I’d defend **paid shadow shifts** so new access agents can hear a real locked-out caller.
I’d insist on **account verification** before fast answers.
think: I think I can **earn and save** before 2036.
I know **cheap thinking AI** may still take my desk.
do: Keep **leading access calls** and save a fixed amount from each wage.
Seek **posted security work** after 2036 if hours fall, with written mortgage-covering weekly wage and hours; stay until signed offer.
Relocate only with a **signed offer** leaving mortgage money after travel and housing costs; keep the children’s school.
feel: **Uneasy** about 2036 and worried about current bills.
S4.quote: A decade before AGI helps only if I still bring a wage home each week.
fieldNote: He values **paid shadow shifts** as practical training.
His **thin cushion** keeps present bills salient.
A family move needs a **signed offer** and net mortgage-covering pay.

steps.text: Keep leading access calls and checking the account record
Save a fixed amount from each wage for the mortgage
Seek posted security work if hours fall with written mortgage-covering pay/hours; stay until signed offer
Relocate only with signed offer leaving mortgage money after travel/housing; keep children’s school

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most: my best calls may become cheap software before we can save enough to search. A posted paid opening with written weekly wage and hours that cover the mortgage, and required training funded on paid time, would help. I would also need notice early enough to ask family for a short, clearly bounded bridge if the first pay is delayed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what happens to the trainee who has never heard a real locked-out customer. A paid first shift beside an experienced agent teaches more than a folder of perfect sample chats.

headlineQuote: A paid first shift beside an experienced agent teaches more than a folder of perfect sample chats.
portrait: At **43**, Gareth leads difficult access calls after a two-year college diploma but receives low pay.
He and Tessa support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with three weeks saved.
He uses **AI daily** while checking account records himself.
He favours **paid practical training**, real vacancies and a bounded family bridge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his strongest calls before he can save for a search.
whatWouldHelp: A **posted mortgage-covering role**, required funded paid-time training, early notice and bounded family help would help.
